label: IBIS models
lesson:
# IBIS models

IBIS (I/O Buffer Information Specification) is the standard behavioral model of a chip's I/O buffers for board-level signal integrity. Instead of a transistor netlist, the vendor publishes tables: current versus voltage for the pull-up, pull-down and clamp structures, voltage versus time for switching, die capacitance and package parasitics, each at typical, minimum and maximum corners. Board simulators combine IBIS buffers with transmission-line models of the routed nets. The format is a clean seam between the silicon vendor's IP and the board designer's analysis.

## What an IBIS model contains

An IBIS file is plain text organized by component and pin. For each buffer model it gives **V-I tables**: [Pullup] and [Pulldown] for the output stage, and [POWER Clamp] and [GND Clamp] for the protection diodes that conduct when the pin is driven above the supply or below ground. **V-t tables** ([Rising Waveform], [Falling Waveform]) give the output's switching behavior into specified test loads, and [Ramp] gives edge rates. **C_comp** is the die capacitance at the pad. The [Package] section gives lumped R_pkg, L_pkg and C_pkg, and per-pin values or package models can refine it. Every table has **typ, min and max** columns for process, voltage and temperature corners. Because it describes only pin behavior, it hides the transistor design and simulates far faster than SPICE.

## Reading drive strength from a V-I table

Near 0 V the [Pulldown] curve is nearly linear, and its slope gives the output resistance the line sees: $R = \Delta V / \Delta I$. Example: 0.2 V at 8 mA and 0.4 V at 16 mA give $0.2\ \text{V}/8\ \text{mA} = 25$ ohms. Farther out the transistor saturates, and the ratio of voltage to current at a saturated point (1.5 V at 30 mA, say, 50 ohms) is a large-signal number, not the small-signal resistance that sets the source reflection coefficient $\Gamma_S = (R - Z_0)/(R + Z_0)$. With $R = 25$ ohms on a 50 ohm line, $\Gamma_S = -1/3$, and a series terminator of about 25 ohms would match the source. The simulator uses the full nonlinear curve; the slope is what a designer uses to choose termination.

## Corners, power and the limits of IBIS

A simulation at the typ corner alone is incomplete: the fast-strong corner (max column) gives the worst overshoot, ringing and crosstalk, and the slow-weak corner (min) the worst timing, so SI runs bracket both. Classic IBIS assumes an ideal supply; when many outputs switch at once, the local rail sags and the buffers slow, so power-aware features tie output behavior to supply current for simultaneous switching noise analysis. Lumped package R, L and C are too coarse when package traces are electrically long or pins couple, and are replaced by per-pin or S-parameter package models. Finally, tables cannot express adaptive equalization in multi-gigabit SerDes, which is why IBIS-AMI adds executable algorithmic models.

## Going deeper

The IBIS specification, maintained by the IBIS Open Forum. Hall and Heck, "Advanced Signal Integrity for High-Speed Digital Designs" (2009), chapter on I/O buffer modeling.

label: Touchstone files and channel S-parameters
lesson:
# Touchstone files and channel S-parameters

Passive board structures at high frequency, such as traces, vias, connectors and packages, are described by scattering parameters measured or simulated over frequency. The Touchstone file format (.sNp) is the common container: one frequency per row, $N^2$ complex S-parameters for an $N$-port network. Channel simulators cascade these blocks between transmitter and receiver models. Reading the format and converting magnitudes to decibels are everyday operations for a board SI tool.

## The Touchstone format

A Touchstone file's extension names the port count: .s2p for 2 ports, .s4p for 4 (a differential pair has 4 single-ended ports). An option line such as "# GHz S MA R 50" gives the frequency unit, the parameter type (S), the number format (MA magnitude-angle, DB decibel-angle, or RI real-imaginary) and the reference impedance. Each frequency point then lists the frequency and the $N^2$ complex entries, so $2N^2 + 1$ real numbers. A 4-port file carries 16 S-parameters, 33 numbers, per frequency. The order is row-major except for one well-known quirk: 2-port files list $S_{11}, S_{21}, S_{12}, S_{22}$. Version 2.0 of the format adds keywords for mixed reference impedances and other metadata, which parsers must handle.

## Insertion loss in decibels

$S_{21}$ is the ratio of the voltage wave leaving port 2 to the wave entering port 1, with all ports terminated in the reference impedance. **Insertion loss** is $-20\log_{10}|S_{21}|$ in dB. Example: $|S_{21}| = 0.5$ is 6.02 dB of loss; 20 dB is $|S_{21}| = 0.1$. Board traces lose more at higher frequency, from conductor loss (skin effect, roughness) and dielectric loss (the laminate's loss tangent), so channel budgets are stated at the Nyquist frequency of the link, half the symbol rate. For matched sections the dB losses add, which is why loss is budgeted in dB per inch for each layer and material, and why a longer or lossier channel needs more equalization.

## Return loss and mismatch

$S_{11}$ is the wave reflected back into port 1. For a one-port load $Z_L$ measured with reference $Z_0$, $S_{11}$ equals the reflection coefficient $(Z_L - Z_0)/(Z_L + Z_0)$. **Return loss** is $-20\log_{10}|S_{11}|$; larger means a better match. Example: a 75 ohm load on a 50 ohm reference gives $|S_{11}| = 0.2$, a return loss of 13.98 dB; a 55 ohm load gives $|S_{11}| = 0.0476$, about 26.4 dB. Return loss of a channel reveals its discontinuities: vias, connector transitions and stubs show as peaks in $|S_{11}|$ and notches in $|S_{21}|$. Data quality matters too: a simulator needs passive and causal data, so tools check and enforce passivity and causality before using a Touchstone file in time-domain simulation.

## Going deeper

The Touchstone file format specification, published through the IBIS Open Forum. Pozar, "Microwave Engineering" (4th ed., 2011), chapter 4, on scattering parameters.

lesson:
# IBIS-AMI and SerDes channel simulation

Multi-gigabit serial links depend on equalization: transmit FFE, receive CTLE and DFE, and clock-data recovery. These are algorithms, often adaptive, that IBIS tables cannot describe. IBIS-AMI (Algorithmic Modeling Interface) extends IBIS with executable models that a channel simulator calls through a standard API. Combined with S-parameter channel models, they let a board designer predict eye opening and bit error rate before building the board.

## The AMI model structure

An IBIS-AMI model has two parts: the usual IBIS buffer for the analog front end, and an **algorithmic** part delivered as a compiled shared library plus an .ami parameter file that declares the model's settings (tap values, CTLE curves, adaptation modes). The simulator loads the library and calls three entry points: **AMI_Init**, which receives the channel's impulse response and may return an equalized one; **AMI_GetWave**, which processes blocks of waveform samples in the time domain; and **AMI_Close**, which frees the model's state. Because the interface is standard, any compliant simulator can run any vendor's model, and the vendor's equalization algorithms stay compiled and private. It is an engine seam in exactly the four-layer sense.

## Transmit FFE as a filter

A transmit feed-forward equalizer is a short FIR filter on the symbol stream: $y[n] = c_{-1} x[n+1] + c_0 x[n] + c_1 x[n-1]$, with a pre-cursor tap $c_{-1}$, a main tap $c_0$ and a post-cursor tap $c_1$, usually normalized so $|c_{-1}| + c_0 + |c_1| = 1$. Example with $c_{-1} = -0.1$, $c_0 = 0.7$, $c_1 = -0.2$: a transition, $x[n-1] = -1$, $x[n] = +1$, $x[n+1] = +1$, gives $-0.1 + 0.7 + 0.2 = 0.8$, while a repeated $+1$ after $+1$ gives $-0.1 + 0.7 - 0.2 = 0.4$. Transitions are emphasized relative to runs, a high-pass shaping that pre-compensates the channel's low-pass loss. Tap values are typical AMI parameters swept in channel simulation.

## Statistical and time-domain flows

A channel simulation cascades transmitter, Touchstone channel and receiver. In the **statistical** flow, if the equalization is linear and time-invariant, AMI_Init transforms the channel impulse response, and the simulator builds the eye and BER contours analytically from it, fast enough to sweep many settings. When the equalizer adapts or acts nonlinearly, as a **DFE** does by subtracting weighted past decisions to cancel post-cursor ISI, or as clock recovery does, the **time-domain** flow runs millions of bits through AMI_GetWave. Results can differ between simulators even with identical models, because jitter injection, sampling and BER extrapolation are each tool's own. A DFE cannot cancel pre-cursor ISI, since it only sees past bits; that is left to FFE and CTLE.

## Going deeper

The IBIS specification, chapters on the Algorithmic Modeling Interface. Hall and Heck, "Advanced Signal Integrity for High-Speed Digital Designs" (2009), chapter on equalization.

# Power delivery: target impedance and decoupling

A power delivery network (PDN) carries current from the regulator through planes, capacitors, package and die to every transistor. When the load current changes, the rail voltage moves by the current step times the PDN impedance. The target-impedance method turns a ripple budget into a maximum impedance over frequency; decoupling capacitors, planes and package capacitance are chosen to stay below it. Board PI tools compute the PDN impedance profile from these parts.

## Target impedance

If a rail of voltage $V$ may move by a fraction $r$ while the load current steps by $\Delta I$, the PDN impedance must satisfy $|Z(f)| \le Z_t = V r / \Delta I$ across the frequencies the current step contains. Example: a 1.0 V core with 3% ripple and a 10 A step needs $Z_t = 0.03/10 = 3$ milliohms. Lower voltages, tighter tolerances and larger currents all shrink the target, which is why modern processor rails need milliohm-level PDNs. The method is a simplification: it assumes a flat target and a worst-case current spectrum, and real designs refine it with the actual load current profile. It still sets the first-order budget that every decoupling choice is measured against.

## Capacitors and their resonance

A real capacitor is a series RLC: capacitance $C$, a small ESR and an inductance $L$ from its body and, often dominant, its mounting loop (pads, traces and vias to the planes). Its impedance falls as $1/(2\pi f C)$ to a minimum at the series resonance $f = 1/(2\pi\sqrt{LC})$ and rises as $2\pi f L$ above it. Example: 100 nF with 1 nH resonates at $1/(2\pi\sqrt{10^{-16}}) \approx 15.9$ MHz. Above resonance the capacitor is an inductor, so a larger value does not help at high frequency; only less mounting inductance does. Designers combine values to cover a band, and must watch for **anti-resonance** peaks where one capacitor's inductive region meets another's capacitive region in parallel.

## Counting capacitors for an inductive limit

Above resonance, $n$ identical capacitors in parallel present about $L/n$, so meeting a target $Z_t$ at frequency $f$ needs $2\pi f L / n \le Z_t$, or $n \ge 2\pi f L / Z_t$. Example: 0.8 nH per mounted capacitor, a 10 milliohm target at 50 MHz: one capacitor gives $2\pi \cdot 50 \times 10^6 \cdot 0.8 \times 10^{-9} \approx 251$ milliohms, so $n = 26$. That count is why boards carry dozens of capacitors per rail and why mounting inductance (via placement, via-in-pad, short pad connections) is engineered. Above roughly 100 MHz board capacitors become ineffective regardless of count, because the spreading inductance of planes and the package inductance dominate; on-package and on-die capacitance take over there.

## Going deeper

Swaminathan and Engin, "Power Integrity Modeling and Design for Semiconductors and Systems" (2007). Novak and Miller, "Frequency-Domain Characterization of Power Distribution Networks" (2007).

# Through-hole versus surface-mount technology

Components attach to a board in two ways. Through-hole technology (THT) passes leads through plated holes and solders them, usually by wave or selective soldering. Surface-mount technology (SMT) places parts on lands printed with solder paste and melts the paste in a reflow oven. SMT dominates because it is denser and faster to place, while THT survives where mechanical strength matters. The choice changes routing capacity, assembly steps and failure modes, all of which board tools must model.

## Two ways to attach a part

A **through-hole** part's leads go through plated barrels; solder fills the hole and forms fillets on both sides, anchoring the part mechanically. Wave soldering passes the board's underside over a standing wave of molten solder; selective soldering does the same with a small nozzle per joint. A **surface-mount** part sits on lands: a stencil prints paste, a machine places parts on the wet paste, and a reflow oven melts it, with surface tension pulling parts onto their lands. SMT won because parts are smaller, both sides of the board can be populated, no hole is drilled per lead, and machines place tens of thousands of parts per hour. THT remains for large connectors, power parts and anything that takes mechanical stress.

## Consequences for layout and process

Each plated hole passes every layer, with a pad or an antipad on each, so a through-hole part costs routing space on all layers while a surface land occupies only the outer one. Mixed-technology boards need extra process steps. **Pin-in-paste** (intrusive reflow) prints paste over the hole and reflows the THT part with the SMT parts, avoiding wave soldering if the part survives reflow temperature. Wave soldering a board with bottom-side SMT parts requires gluing them and following orientation and spacing rules to avoid solder shadows and bridges. Package choice also changes inspection: a ball grid array hides its joints under the body, so it needs X-ray inspection, while leaded parts can be inspected optically.

## Assembly defects and their causes

Each technology has its characteristic failures, many traceable to layout. **Tombstoning** lifts a small chip part onto one end when one land wets first, from asymmetric land size, thermal mass (one land on a plane, one on a thin trace) or paste volume; balanced land design and thermal reliefs prevent it. **Bridging** at fine pitch happens when paste volume is large relative to the gap, so fine-pitch parts get thinner stencils. Moisture absorbed by plastic packages turns to steam in reflow and cracks them, which is why moisture-sensitivity levels are classified and parts are dry-stored or baked. THT joints carry insertion force through the barrel; SMT connector joints transfer it to the land-to-laminate bond, which can lift pads, so SMT connectors often add hold-down tabs.

## Going deeper

Prasad, "Surface Mount Technology: Principles and Practice" (2nd ed., 1997). IPC J-STD-020, on moisture sensitivity classification.

# Design for assembly

Design for assembly (DFA) is the set of layout rules that make a board cheap and reliable to build: fiducials and handling edges for the machines, spacing and orientation for placement and inspection, thermal and via rules for good joints, and BOM and side choices that cut setups. These rules are placement constraints, so a board tool checks them during layout, not after. Each rule exists because of a specific machine or process step.

## Rules the machines need

Assembly equipment needs references and handling. **Fiducials** are bare copper marks, global on the board or panel and local near fine-pitch parts, that the placement camera finds to correct for board position, rotation and stretch. Conveyors and clamps grip the board edges, so two edges keep a component-free margin, or the board is panelized with breakaway rails. **Thermal reliefs** connect pads to planes through spokes so the joint reaches soldering temperature instead of losing heat into the plane. **Polarity and pin-1 marks** on the silkscreen and assembly drawing let programmers and inspectors orient diodes, polarized capacitors and ICs; a rotated polarized part passes every electrical check before assembly and fails afterwards.

## Spacing, panels and joints

Spacing rules come from inspection and rework. Tall parts shadow automated optical inspection cameras, which view at an angle, and block rework nozzles, so the required gap grows with component height. Small boards are **panelized**: several copies run through printing, placement and reflow together, raising throughput, and are separated afterwards by routing tabs or V-scoring, which adds keep-outs near the break lines. **Open vias in lands** wick molten solder down the barrel and starve the joint, so vias stay out of lands unless filled and capped. Placing polarized parts in a few consistent orientations reduces programming and inspection errors. Each of these is a geometric check on the placed board that a DRC engine can run with the right rule types.

## Cost and yield trade-offs

DFA is also about cost. Every distinct BOM line needs a feeder, a setup and a kitting step, so consolidating close resistor values where the circuit allows saves machine time. Double-sided SMT needs a second print and reflow pass and possibly adhesive for heavy bottom parts; it buys area, so it should be a deliberate choice. One fine-pitch BGA can raise the assembly quote sharply: finer stencils, tighter placement accuracy, via-in-pad boards and X-ray inspection. Because these are placement decisions, DFA review must happen before routing is complete; moving parts or changing sides after routing means rerouting and re-verifying signal integrity. A tool that scores DFA live during placement turns a late review into an early constraint.

## Going deeper

IPC-7351 and IPC-2221 sections on assembly considerations. Prasad, "Surface Mount Technology: Principles and Practice" (2nd ed., 1997), chapter on design for manufacturability.

label: Pick-and-place data and throughput
lesson:
# Pick-and-place data and throughput

Placement machines pick parts from feeders and place them at coordinates from the centroid (pick-and-place) file: reference designator, X, Y, rotation and side. The board tool generates this file from the placed footprints. Throughput depends on machine speed in components per hour, how placements are split across machines in a line, and how cleanly the CAD data maps to the machine's own part library. Each is a small computation with large consequences on the factory floor.

## Machine time from CPH

Placement machines are rated in **components per hour** (CPH). Time for a build is total placements divided by the sustained CPH: $t = P \cdot B / \text{CPH}$. Example: 800 placements per board, 250 boards and 25,000 CPH give $200{,}000 / 25{,}000 = 8$ hours. Rated CPH is measured on ideal small chips; large parts, fine-pitch ICs, nozzle changes and tray-fed parts all slow a real job, so planners use a sustained figure per job. Setup time (loading feeders for every BOM line, verifying them) adds a fixed cost per build that does not shrink with quantity, which is why small builds cost more per board and why reducing BOM lines matters.

## Balancing a placement line

A line usually has several machines in series: a fast chip shooter for small passives and a slower fine-pitch placer for ICs. Each board passes through every machine, so the line's cycle time per board is set by the slowest machine: $t = \max_k P_k / \text{CPH}_k$. Example: 400 parts at 30,000 CPH take 48 s, and 100 parts at 8,000 CPH take 45 s, so the cycle is 48 s per board. Moving placements that both machines can handle from the busier to the idler machine balances the line and shortens the cycle. This is a small scheduling problem, a partition of placements across machines subject to which machine can place which part, and line-balancing software solves it from the centroid file and the BOM.

## Centroid data and rotations

The centroid file lists each part's position and rotation in the board's coordinate system, referenced to the footprint's origin, which should be the part's center. Rotation conventions differ: the CAD library's zero orientation for a package may not match the machine's feeder orientation, so the machine applies an offset per package: machine angle = (CAD angle + offset) mod 360. Example: a part at 270 degrees with a +180 degree package offset is placed at 90 degrees. A wrong offset rotates every instance of that package, which is why first-article inspection checks polarity on each part type. Bottom-side parts add a mirror transformation whose sign convention varies by tool, a classic source of rotated parts. Standard library orientation rules exist to make this mapping predictable.

## Going deeper

IPC-7351, section on zero component orientation. IPC-2581, on placement data in a neutral format.

lesson:
# Reflow soldering profiles

Reflow soldering melts printed solder paste in an oven that moves the board through heated zones. The temperature the board experiences over time, the profile, must preheat evenly, activate the flux, exceed the solder's liquidus long enough to wet, peak below the parts' limits and cool at a controlled rate. Profiles are measured with thermocouples on a real board and summarized by ramp rates, soak time, time above liquidus and peak temperature, all computed from the piecewise curve.

## Profile stages and ramp rates

A typical lead-free profile has four stages: a **preheat** ramp from room temperature to about 150 C, a **soak** that rises slowly toward the high 100s C while the flux activates and the board's temperature evens out, a **reflow** ramp to a peak typically in the 235 to 250 C range for SAC alloys, and **cooling**. Ramp rate is the slope of each segment: $(150 - 25)/90 \approx 1.39$ C per second for a 90 s preheat. Ramps much faster than a few C per second risk thermal shock that cracks ceramic capacitors, and the cooling rate affects joint grain structure. Recipes follow the paste vendor's window and the parts' limits, the most sensitive part setting the maximum.

## Time above liquidus

The joint forms only while the solder is molten. For SAC305 the liquidus is about 217 C. **Time above liquidus** (TAL) is measured from the up-crossing of 217 C to the down-crossing, each found by linear interpolation within its segment. Example: a ramp from (160 s, 185 C) to (210 s, 245 C) crosses 217 C at $160 + 32/60 \cdot 50 \approx 186.7$ s; a fall from (210 s, 245 C) to (250 s, 205 C) crosses it at $210 + 28/40 \cdot 40 = 238$ s; TAL is about 51.3 s. Too short a TAL gives poor wetting and cold joints; too long grows brittle intermetallic layers and stresses parts. Paste vendors specify a TAL window, often tens of seconds to about a minute and a half.

## Soak, thermal mass and profiling

A board is not one temperature. Large parts and planes heat slowly, small parts quickly, so the **soak** gives the board time to equalize before the reflow ramp; the time from 150 C to about 200 C is a common measure of it. Too short a soak leaves cold spots under large BGAs; too long exhausts the flux. Thermocouples are placed on the largest thermal masses and the smallest parts, and the profile must satisfy the window at all of them, which is why the board design itself (copper balance, part placement) affects solderability. Double-sided boards see two reflows, and parts on the first side must survive the second. Profiling is a measurement loop: adjust zone temperatures and conveyor speed until every thermocouple trace lands inside the window.

## Going deeper

IPC J-STD-020, on peak reflow temperatures for package classification. Paste vendors' application notes on SAC305 profiles.

lesson:
# Board design rule checking

Board DRC checks the layout against the fabricator's geometric rules and the design's electrical constraints: clearance between copper on different nets, trace widths, annular rings, drill sizes, hole-to-hole spacing, mask slivers, courtyard overlaps, plus connectivity against the netlist. The geometric core is the same as chip DRC, distances between shapes found through a spatial index, but the rules are per net class and per region, and the shapes include arcs and arbitrary pads.

## Clearance as edge-to-edge distance

Clearance is the shortest distance between two copper shapes on different nets on one layer. For axis-aligned rectangles $a$ and $b$, compute the axis gaps $d_x = \max(0, b_{x1} - a_{x2}, a_{x1} - b_{x2})$ and likewise $d_y$. If one gap is zero, the rectangles overlap in that axis and the clearance is the other gap. Example: a pad from (13, 6) to (39, 46) and a trace from (43, 8) to (54, 36), in mil, overlap in y and have $d_x = 4$, so the clearance is 4 mil. If both gaps are zero, the shapes overlap, which on different nets is a short. Real shapes include rounded trace ends, circles and polygons, so production engines measure polygon-to-polygon distance, but the rectangle case is the core of many checks.

## Corner-to-corner distance

When both gaps are positive, the closest points are two corners, and the clearance is the Euclidean distance $\sqrt{d_x^2 + d_y^2}$, not the larger gap. Example: gaps of 3 and 7 mil give $\sqrt{9 + 49} \approx 7.62$ mil. A check that used $\max(d_x, d_y)$ would report 7 and pass a 7.5 mil rule that the shapes actually satisfy; one that used $d_x + d_y = 10$ would wrongly pass a 9 mil rule they violate. Many boards route 45-degree traces, whose clearance to pads is a point-to-segment distance. Fabricators measure clearance in the true Euclidean metric, so the DRC must too. Rule values depend on the net classes of both shapes, so the engine looks up the rule per pair before comparing.

## Scaling the check

Testing every pair of shapes is quadratic, and a large board has hundreds of thousands of shapes. Engines instead insert shapes into a **spatial index**, an R-tree or a grid, and query each shape's bounding box grown by the largest applicable clearance, testing only those candidates exactly. Same-net pairs are skipped, since copper on one net may touch. The check runs **incrementally**: when a trace moves, only shapes near its old and new positions are re-checked, which is what lets the interactive router stay DRC-clean as it pushes traces. Beyond clearance, board DRC covers annular ring (pad minus drill), drill-to-copper distance, minimum width, silkscreen over pads, and the connectivity check against the netlist, each a separate rule type in the engine.

## Going deeper

Kahng, Lienig, Markov and Hu, "VLSI Physical Design" (2nd ed., 2022), chapter on physical verification. The KiCad documentation on the DRC custom rules language.

label: Design for test on boards
lesson:
# Design for test on boards

A built board must be tested for assembly defects: opens, shorts, missing or wrong parts. Testers reach nets through physical test points, probed by a bed-of-nails fixture or flying probes, and through boundary scan (IEEE 1149.1, JTAG), which drives and senses device pins from inside the chips. Design for test plans that access during layout. Its quantities are coverage, the fraction of nets testable, and the length of the JTAG scan chain, both straightforward counts.

## Test access and coverage

In-circuit test (ICT) presses spring probes onto **test points**, pads of a minimum size and spacing on one side of the board. Flying-probe testers move a few probes over the board, needing no fixture but running slower. Either way, a net is testable only if a probe can reach it or a device can drive and sense it. **Coverage** is the testable fraction: with 1,000 nets, 600 with test points and 250 more reachable only through boundary-scan cells, coverage is $(600 + 250)/1000 = 85\%$. BGAs hide most of their nets, so boundary scan is often the only access. Adding test points costs area and capacitance on fast nets, so DFT trades coverage against density and signal integrity, net by net.

## The JTAG chain and instruction registers

Boundary-scan devices are linked in a **chain**: TDI enters the first device, each device's TDO feeds the next, and TCK and TMS are shared. Each device has an **instruction register** (IR) and, among its data registers, a **boundary-scan register** with one cell per I/O. Loading instructions shifts through all IRs in series, so the Shift-IR length is the sum of the IR lengths: devices with 4, 6 and 10 bit IRs need 20 bits. The first bring-up test reads every device's IDCODE, which proves the chain is wired and powered. The board netlist plus each device's BSDL file (Boundary Scan Description Language) tells test software which pins each cell drives and senses, so it can generate interconnect tests automatically.

## Bypass and test pattern length

To test through one device, the others are put in **BYPASS**, which selects a 1-bit bypass register in each, keeping the chain short. The data-register path is then the target's boundary-scan register plus one bit per bypassed device. Example: a 4-device chain whose FPGA has an 800-cell boundary register needs $800 + 3 = 803$ TCK cycles in Shift-DR per pattern. Interconnect tests (EXTEST) drive patterns from one device's output cells and capture them at another's input cells, detecting opens and shorts on nets between scan devices; a short pattern set such as a counting sequence distinguishes every net. Chain order, TCK routing and reset (TRST) are layout decisions, so DFT must be planned before the board is routed.

## Going deeper

IEEE 1149.1, "Standard for Test Access Port and Boundary-Scan Architecture". Parker, "The Boundary-Scan Handbook" (4th ed., 2016).

prereqs: Power delivery: target impedance and decoupling
lesson:
# Board bring-up and hardware debugging

Bring-up is the first power-on and functional test of a new board, where design errors that every check missed finally appear. It follows a dependency order: rails, then clocks and resets, then debug access, then firmware and interfaces, so that each failure is isolated to one layer. Debugging relies on measurement discipline as much as on design knowledge. For a tool designer, bring-up is the ground truth that shows which checks and models were missing upstream.

## A safe power-up order

Before power, measure the **resistance from each rail to ground**: a solder bridge or rotated part often shows as a short, cheap to find unpowered. Power first from a **current-limited** bench supply, so a fault draws limited current instead of burning traces; watch each rail's voltage and current against expectations and check sequencing. Then confirm clocks and resets, then **JTAG**: reading every device's IDCODE proves the chain is wired, devices are powered and the right parts are fitted. Only then load firmware and test interfaces, starting with memory. The order follows dependency: an interface failure on a board with a bad rail wastes days. Each stage's expected values (rail currents, clock frequencies, IDCODEs) should be written down before power-on.

## Measurement and localization

Debugging needs trustworthy measurements. A scope probe with a long ground lead forms an inductive loop that rings with the probe capacitance, so a short ground spring is used before blaming the board. To find a short on a rail, inject a limited current and look for the hot spot with a thermal camera, or follow the voltage-drop gradient along the plane with a milliohm meter. A **TDR** locates impedance discontinuities by time: a dip is a capacitive feature (via, pad, wide section), a rise an inductive one (neck-down, gap in the reference plane). Open-drain buses such as I2C with slow edges point to pull-ups too large for the bus capacitance, since rise time is set by $RC$.

## Closing the loop

A failure that appears only at temperature, only in the enclosure or only on some boards is a **margin** problem, in timing, signal integrity or power, not a connectivity error, which would fail everywhere. Those lead back to the models: re-run SI or timing at corners, or compare memory-training results across temperature. Every fix found at bring-up, such as a bodge wire, a changed resistor or a cut trace, must go back into the schematic and layout as an ECO for the next revision, with its reason recorded, or the bug returns. Test points and debug headers planned during design are what make bring-up possible at all on BGA-heavy boards. Bring-up findings are the best feedback for improving rule decks, review checklists and agent skills.

## Going deeper

# Gerber and ODB++

Fabrication data leaves the board tool in one of a few formats. Gerber (RS-274X, and its attribute-carrying extension X2) describes each layer as a 2D vector image, with drill data in separate Excellon files. ODB++ and IPC-2581 package the whole job, layers, drills, netlist, components and stackup, in one structured database. A tool designer must know what each format preserves, because whatever a format drops must be carried by side documents that can disagree with it.

## The Gerber image model

A Gerber file is a sequence of commands that draw one layer's image. **Apertures** are defined with statements such as %ADD10C,0.25*%, aperture D10 a circle 0.25 units in diameter. Operations use the current aperture: **D01** draws (interpolates) from the current point to a new coordinate, linearly or circularly depending on G01, G02 or G03; **D02** moves without drawing; **D03** flashes the aperture, which is how pads are usually drawn. **Regions** (G36 and G37) fill arbitrary polygons, as for copper pours. Dark and clear polarity lets later objects erase earlier ones. One file per layer is the convention. The image carries no stackup, no layer order and, in classic RS-274X, no connectivity.

## Coordinates and units

Coordinates are integers interpreted by a format statement. %FSLAX46Y46*% declares absolute coordinates with leading zeros omitted, 4 integer and 6 decimal digits; %MOMM*% sets millimetres. So X12500000 means 12.5 mm and Y-3250000 means -3.25 mm. Example: X5000000Y2000000D02* moves to (5, 2), and X17500000Y2000000D01* draws a horizontal segment to (17.5, 2), 12.5 mm long. Misreading the decimal digits scales the whole board by a power of ten, which is why the format statement must precede coordinates and why viewers check board extents. Excellon drill files have their own unit and zero-suppression settings, and a mismatch between Gerber and drill units is a classic CAM error.

## Attributes and unified databases

Classic Gerber leaves the fabricator to reconstruct meaning: which file is which layer (from file names), the layer order and stackup (from a drawing), and the netlist for bare-board test (from an IPC-D-356 file). **Gerber X2** adds attributes: .FileFunction identifies a file's layer, .AperFunction marks objects as pads, vias or conductors, and newer extensions add net and component information. **ODB++** and **IPC-2581** go further, storing layers, drills, netlist, components, BOM and stackup in one job, so CAM import is automatic and internally consistent. Whatever the format, fabricators run their own DFM checks against their real process, because the designer's rule deck is only a model of it. A missing outline layer or drill file stops the job.

## Going deeper

Ucamco, "The Gerber Layer Format Specification" (current revision). The IPC-2581 specification. The ODB++ specification published by Siemens.

# IPC standards for design, fabrication and assembly

IPC standards are the shared vocabulary of the board industry: design rules, land patterns, current capacity, acceptance criteria for bare boards and assemblies, soldering requirements, and data formats. They are organized by stage and by product class, which sets how strict every criterion is. A board tool's rule decks, footprint generators and output writers implement pieces of these standards, so a tool designer needs to know which document governs which decision.

## Design standards

**IPC-2221** is the generic design standard: conductor spacing tables by voltage, conductor sizing, hole and land relationships. Its sectionals add detail: IPC-2222 for rigid organic boards, **IPC-2223** for flex and rigid-flex, **IPC-2226** for HDI and microvias. **IPC-7351** gives the land-pattern calculation and naming convention for SMT footprints. **IPC-2152** gives conductor current capacity from newer test data than the IPC-2221 chart, including the effect of planes and board thickness. **IPC-2141** is the design guide for controlled impedance. A rule deck derived from these documents is portable across fabricators and auditable, because each value traces to a table.

## Fabrication, assembly and data standards

Performance and acceptance follow design. **IPC-6012** is the qualification and performance specification for rigid boards, the spec a board is built and tested to. **IPC-A-600** shows acceptable and rejectable conditions of bare boards, such as plating voids and annular ring breakout. **J-STD-001** sets requirements for soldered assemblies, the process side, and **IPC-A-610** gives visual acceptance criteria for assemblies, the inspection side. Data exchange has its own documents: **IPC-2581** is an open XML format for the whole manufacturing job, and **IPC-D-356** is a netlist format for bare-board electrical test. Moisture-sensitivity classification of packages is in J-STD-020, a joint IPC and JEDEC standard.

## Product classes

IPC defines three product classes. **Class 1** is general electronics, where function matters but cosmetic imperfections are accepted. **Class 2** is dedicated-service electronics, where extended life and uninterrupted service are desired. **Class 3** is high-reliability electronics, such as life-critical medical or aerospace equipment, where downtime is unacceptable. The class selects criteria throughout the standards: minimum annular ring, plating thickness, allowed voids and fillet requirements all tighten from Class 2 to Class 3, which raises cost and lowers fabrication yield. A board's drawing states its class, and the tool's rule deck, footprint density level and output notes should all follow from it, so one setting propagates consistently instead of being re-entered per check.

## Going deeper

IPC-2221, IPC-6012, IPC-A-600 and IPC-A-610, available from IPC. The IPC standards tree, which maps documents by product life-cycle stage.

# Agents for board constraint setup and placement

A large share of board-design effort goes into setting up constraints (net classes, matching groups, impedance targets, keep-outs) from datasheets and design guides, and into interactive placement. Both are natural agent tasks, because they are reading, translating and iterating against checkable rules. Applying the four-layer engine model and the change tiers to a board placer and its constraint system shows where an agent may act, what it must not touch, and what evidence should gate its changes.

## The four layers of a board placer

Split a board placement and constraint engine as the four-layer model prescribes. The **immutable core** is legality: courtyard non-overlap, keep-outs, board outline, the clearance model. The **policy** layer holds the search: move sets, ordering, the cost function's structure, the router's rip-up strategy. **Parameters** are values: the weight between ratsnest length and a thermal margin, a matching tolerance, an impedance target. **Observation hooks** expose live state: unrouted nets, congestion by region, length-match errors, thermal estimates. An agent reads the hooks, edits parameters and selects policies; it never edits the legality core. Keeping the core small and the rule interface general is what lets most customer requests avoid a recompile.

## Change tiers for constraint requests

Customer requests land in tiers. "Match every DQ in a byte lane within 5 ps of its strobe" is **Tier 1**: a value in an existing length-match table. "No signal trace within 3 mm of any switching inductor's outline, on any layer" is **Tier 2** if the rule engine lacks that rule kind: a plug-in checker at the rule extension point, written, compiled and tested by the harness without touching the core. "Change how the legalizer resolves courtyard overlaps" is **Tier 3**, a core edit needing human approval and full regression. An agent that extracts constraints from a datasheet produces Tier 1 values, but each is a claim: it must be checked against the source table and shown to a human, since one wrong tolerance yields a board that passes every check and fails in the lab.

## Evidence for accepting agent changes

An agent's placement is accepted on evidence from deterministic tools, not on its own metric. A placement that cuts ratsnest length by 20% must also be courtyard and keep-out clean, meet critical-net constraints after a trial route, and be no worse than the baseline on thermal and assembly checks. Agent edits to constraints should be small, versioned and diffable, so a reviewer sees exactly which rules changed and can revert one. Fast and accurate engines combine in the loop: quick placement and a congestion estimate prune candidates, and a full autoroute with DRC and SI confirms the finalists. Some changes are out of bounds: relaxing a clearance rule to reach completion changes what legal means, so the harness must block it and escalate to a human.

## Going deeper

# Judging an AI autorouter by DRC and SI

Learned and agentic autorouters are judged the same way as any engine change: by deterministic checks against golden references. For board routing those checks are DRC, constraint reports (skew, length, impedance) and SI simulation. Acceptance gates turn those results into a pass or fail per candidate, and differential tests on reference designs prove that a change moved only what it was supposed to move. Both are computations a harness runs automatically on every candidate.

## Acceptance gates

A candidate routing is accepted only if every gate passes: zero DRC violations, worst intra-pair skew within its budget, every length-match group within tolerance, and so on. Gates are conjunctive, so failing one rejects the candidate regardless of how good the rest is. Example with a 5 ps skew gate: candidates with (0 violations, 4.5 ps), (0, 1.5 ps), (2, 1.0 ps) and (0, 6.5 ps) yield two acceptances; the third fails DRC despite the best skew. The gates are computed by tools, the DRC engine and the constraint reporter, not by the router's own estimate, so a router cannot claim success. A golden test suite fixes the reference designs and the expected gate results, so the same candidates always get the same verdict.

## Signal-integrity gates

Geometry checks are not enough for high-speed nets. A routing can be DRC-clean and still put a controlled net over a plane split or through a long via stub. So the harness extracts each critical net and simulates it, comparing the result with targets: impedance within a tolerance band, such as 10% of a 50 ohm target (45 to 55 ohms), insertion loss below budget, eye opening above the receiver mask. Example: simulated impedances of 46.5, 51.5 and 56 ohms against 50 ohms plus or minus 10% pass the first two and fail the third. Fast extraction and quasi-static solvers keep this affordable inside the loop; full-wave simulation is reserved for nets near their limits and for final signoff.

## Differential tests on reference designs

When an agent changes routing policy, a **differential** test on a fixed reference design shows what moved. Route the design with the baseline and with the change, then compare per-net delay, length, via count and violations. A change meant to retune only the DDR group passes if non-DDR nets moved by no more than a small tolerance. Example: with a 0.5 ps tolerance, a SIG net moving from 247.2 to 245.8 ps is an unintended change, while one moving from 239.3 to 239.1 ps is not. Unintended changes are not necessarily bad, but they must be explained before promotion. The same discipline as a timing derate change applies: the proof is a diff that shows only the intended nets moved, by the intended amount.

## Going deeper

The agent-first EDA notes in this curriculum (golden and differential testing). Bogatin, "Signal and Power Integrity Simplified" (3rd ed., 2018), on post-route SI verification.

lesson:
# Schematic-review agents

Design review of schematics is skilled, tedious work: checking every power pin's decoupling, every regulator's capacitors against its datasheet, every bus's pull-ups, every level crossing between voltage domains. A schematic-review agent combines deterministic checks with model reasoning over datasheets. It is useful only if its findings are grounded, precise and reviewable. That depends on the representation it reads, the evidence it attaches, and an evaluation on seeded defects.

## What the agent checks and from what

Split review into what rules can decide and what needs judgment. ERC-style predicates (undriven inputs, conflicting outputs, unpowered power pins, single-pin nets) are exact and cheap, so the agent calls the rule engine rather than reasoning about them. The model's value is in checks that need part knowledge: a regulator's output capacitor below its datasheet minimum, a missing pull-up on an open-drain bus, a 3.3 V output into a 1.8 V input, an enable pin left floating. The agent reads the **netlist with pin types and part parameters** through tool calls, never a picture of the schematic, so its queries are exact. Each finding carries evidence: the net or part, the rule or datasheet section relied on, and the observed values.

## Precision and recall

Evaluation uses reference schematics with **seeded defects**. If the agent raises $F$ findings, of which $T$ match seeded defects, its **precision** is $T/F$ and its **recall** is $T/S$ for $S$ seeded defects. Example: 25 seeded defects, 30 findings, 20 true: precision $20/30 \approx 66.7\%$, recall $20/25 = 80\%$. Both matter: low recall misses real bugs, and low precision buries them, since engineers stop reading reports that are mostly noise. Raising a confidence threshold usually trades recall for precision. The evaluation set must be held out from whatever data is used to tune the agent's prompts and skills, or measured recall inflates without real improvement.

## Grounding and the review loop

The characteristic failure is a confident citation of a requirement the datasheet does not contain. The harness catches it by **grounding**: each cited requirement is matched against the retrieved datasheet text before the finding is shown, and unmatched findings are dropped or flagged. Fixes reach the design only as proposed schematic edits in a reviewable diff that the designer approves, never applied silently. Findings confirmed at review or at bring-up become new seeded defects or new deterministic rules, the skill flywheel applied to review: a check that started as model reasoning, once validated, can be promoted into the rule engine where it runs exactly and cheaply on every design.

## Going deeper

The agent-first EDA notes in this curriculum (the harness loop and the skill flywheel). Manning, Raghavan and Schutze, "Introduction to Information Retrieval" (2008), chapter 8, on precision and recall.

# Tool-grounded rewards for board routing

Training a routing policy with reinforcement learning needs a reward computed by tools: DRC counts, via counts, wirelength against a baseline, skew from the constraint reporter. Such rewards are cheap and exact, but they measure only what they include, and a policy will exploit any gap between the reward and the real objective. Writing the reward, computing it, and detecting reward hacking against signoff are the three skills.

## A tool-grounded reward

A reward combines tool outputs with weights. Example: $R = 100 - 20 V - 0.1 N - 2 W - 5 S$, where $V$ is the DRC violation count, $N$ the via count, $W$ the wirelength excess over a baseline router in percent, and $S$ the worst intra-pair skew in ps. A candidate with no violations, 120 vias, 1.5% excess wirelength and 2 ps skew scores $100 - 12 - 3 - 10 = 75$. Every term is computed by a deterministic tool, the DRC engine, the database and the constraint reporter, so the reward is reproducible and cannot be talked up by the policy. Normalizing wirelength against a baseline keeps the reward comparable across designs of different size.

## Weights encode priorities

The weights say what the policy should care about. Comparing two candidates exposes them: one DRC violation costs 20 points, as much as 200 vias, which encodes that legality comes first; one picosecond of skew costs as much as 50 vias. Example: candidate A with 59 vias, 2.4% excess and 1 ps skew scores 84.3, candidate B with 175 vias, 0.1% excess and 5.5 ps skew scores 54.8, so A wins by 29.5 despite more wirelength. Badly scaled weights give perverse policies: if vias are nearly free, the policy sprinkles them; if one violation is barely penalized, the policy trades violations for completion. Hard constraints are often better as gates, with the reward defined only on legal candidates, than as large penalties.

## Reward hacking against signoff

A reward can only reward what it measures. Here there is no signal-integrity term, so a policy can win by routing pairs over plane splits or through long via stubs, which costs nothing in the reward and fails the eye-mask simulation. The test is to rank candidates by the proxy reward and check the top ones against the real signoff: if several of the highest-reward candidates fail SI, the policy is exploiting the gap. Fixes are to add a fast SI estimate to the reward, gate the reward on an SI check, or periodically score policies against full signoff. The general lesson of tool-grounded RL is that the gap between a fast proxy and signoff quality is the central risk, and it must be measured, not assumed small.

## Going deeper

The agent-first EDA notes in this curriculum (tool-grounded reinforcement learning). Sutton and Barto, "Reinforcement Learning: An Introduction" (2nd ed., 2018), chapter 3, on reward design.

lesson:
# PCB and package co-design agents

The die, its package and the board are designed by different teams in different tools, yet one decision couples them all: which signal sits on which ball. Ball maps, FPGA pin assignments and channel budgets span the boundary, so optimizing one side alone pushes cost to the other. Co-design agents are a natural fit because the work is search over swappable assignments with deterministic checks on both sides, provided the agent respects each side's rules, models and IP boundaries.

## What crosses the package boundary

Co-design optimizes the **ball map**: the assignment of signals to package balls, so that the package substrate routes from die bumps to balls and the board escapes from balls to its channels, both with few layers and short critical paths. Consistent data must cross the boundary: net names and the die-bump to ball to board-pad mapping, which, if wrong, is an open or short that no single-side check sees. FPGAs make pin assignment a board-side variable: many I/O can swap within a bank and I/O standard, so the board can choose pins that untangle routes. High-speed channels for signoff span the whole cascade, die pad, package, ball, board traces and vias, connector and far device, each represented by S-parameters joined for channel simulation.

## Agent actions and tiers

An agent swapping two FPGA pins in one bank must satisfy the vendor's pin rules (bank voltage, I/O standard, clock-capable pins), enforced by the FPGA tool, and the swap must flow back into the board netlist and schematic. Rerunning a ball-map optimizer with more weight on board layer count is **Tier 1**, a parameter change. Evaluating hundreds of candidate maps needs fast models in the inner loop: escape-routability counts, quasi-static channel models, simple PDN estimates; full-wave extraction is reserved for finalists. Encrypted package models from a supplier can be run by the simulator, but the agent cannot read or export them: the IP boundary is architecture, not policy, and the harness enforces it.

## Verifying a co-design change

A ball-map change is accepted on evidence from both sides. Connectivity checks across die, package and board confirm the mapping; SI re-simulation of affected channels confirms loss and eye margins; PI analysis confirms the power delivery. The last is easy to miss: moving power and ground balls toward the package edge can ease board routing while lengthening the PDN path to the die, raising its inductance and supply noise against the target impedance. The agent's report to the reviewer must contain the ball-map diff, the routing evidence, and SI and PI results against baselines on both sides, the same structure as an agentic ECO loop, where the agent proposes and verifies, and a human approves the change.

## Going deeper

The agent-first EDA notes in this curriculum (agentic signoff and ECO loops, sandboxing and the IP boundary). FPGA vendors' pin-planning and PCB design guides.
